snip.t: Peutz-Jeghers polyps: characteristic arborising smooth muscle core; part of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (autosomal dominant, mucocutaneous pigmentation, increased risk of GI and extra-GI cancers)
LKB1 tumour suppressor — somatically mutated in >20% of cervical cancers; normally activates AMPK → regulates cell growth via mTOR; also mutated in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and lung cancer

faq.a: Melanin deposition in basal keratinocytes caused by the STK11 mutation; spots appear early and persist.
faq.q: Why do patients develop dark spots on the lips?

faq.a: Yes; while hamartomatous, they can acquire dysplasia and progress to adenocarcinoma, especially when large or numerous.
Not mandatory; clinical criteria suffice, but testing confirms the mutation, guides family screening, and is recommended when resources allow.
faq.q: Is genetic testing mandatory for diagnosis?

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with intermittent abdominal pain and pigmented lip spots – what are the three diagnostic criteria you would apply? — Identify clinical pigmentation, endoscopic polyps, and family history or STK11 mutation.
During endoscopy you find a 3‑cm hamartomatous polyp causing partial obstruction – what is the next best step? — Attempt endoscopic polypectomy; if not feasible, arrange surgical resection.

A patient with known PJS develops new breast tenderness – which surveillance test is preferred and why? — Annual breast MRI (or ultrasound where MRI unavailable) because of high breast‑cancer risk and superior sensitivity.
You suspect intussusception in a child with PJS – which bedside sign helps and what imaging confirms it? — “Currant‑jelly” stool and palpable abdominal mass; ultrasound shows target sign.

Explain why NSAIDs may be used to reduce polyp size in PJS and why they are not first‑line in patients with hypertension. — COX‑2 inhibition can shrink polyps; however, NSAIDs raise blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.
A 35‑year‑old with PJS has normal colonoscopy but ongoing anemia – what further test would you order? — Capsule endoscopy or small‑bowel barium study to look for distal small‑bowel polyps.
Discuss the role of STK11 in cellular pathways and how its loss leads to tumour formation. — STK11 activates AMPK, inhibiting mTOR; loss removes this brake, allowing uncontrolled growth.

What counselling should you give a 20‑year‑old woman with PJS regarding pregnancy? — Discuss increased ovarian cancer risk, need for early ultrasound screening, and that the mutation is autosomal‑dominant, so offspring have 50 % risk.
ai.title: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: An autosomal‑dominant disorder caused by STK11 loss, characterised by hamartomatous GI polyps and mucocutaneous melanin spots, with markedly increased cancer risk.

b: Autosomal‑dominant inheritance (50 % risk to offspring)
STK11/LKB1 germline mutation in >80 % of molecularly confirmed cases
sections.p: Peutz‑Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is a hereditary hamartomatous polyposis syndrome with characteristic mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation and multiple GI polyps. Diagnosis requires two of three criteria: (1) typical pigmented macules on lips, buccal mucosa or perioral skin, (2) ≥2 histologically confirmed hamartomatous polyps, (3) a first‑degree relative with PJS, or a pathogenic STK11 variant.

t.a: Clinical exam of lips and oral mucosa
t.b: Detects characteristic melanin macules; presence supports diagnosis
Identifies hamartomatous polyps; size > 1 cm raises intussusception risk
Confirms hereditary basis; guides family screening

b: Low risk: <5 cm total polyp length, no dysplasia
Moderate risk: 5–10 cm total length or isolated dysplasia
High risk: >10 cm total length, multiple dysplasias, or any cancer
sections.p: Severity is gauged by polyp burden, location, and cancer history rather than a formal stage. The WHO recommends classifying patients as low, moderate, or high risk based on cumulative polyp size (>5 cm) and presence of dysplasia or malignancy.

b: STK11 mutation – disrupts AMPK‑mTOR pathway, promoting uncontrolled cell growth
Co‑existing chronic infections (e.g., Helicobacter pylori) may accelerate polyp inflammation
sections.p: The primary cause is a germline loss‑of‑function mutation in the tumour‑suppressor STK11 (also called LKB1). Secondary contributors include modifier genes and environmental factors such as chronic inflammation from infections common in low‑resource settings.

b: Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation – flat, 2–5 mm macules
Hamartomatous polyps – pedunculated, can cause obstruction
Family history of similar spots or early‑onset cancers
sections.p: Patients often first notice dark freckles on the lips or buccal mucosa in childhood. In adolescence or early adulthood they develop abdominal pain, GI bleeding, or intussusception from large polyps. Extra‑intestinal signs include breast, pancreatic, ovarian, and cervical cancers, often decades later.
A stepwise approach balances diagnostic yield with resource constraints.

t.b: Detects small‑bowel polyps not seen on standard scopes; positive finding prompts surgical referral
Screens for intussusception or large polyps; shows target sign in intussusception

t.a: Serum tumor markers (CA‑125, CEA, CA‑19‑9) in surveillance
t.b: Elevated levels may signal malignant transformation; normal values do not exclude cancer

b: Acute intestinal obstruction or intussusception – sudden severe abdominal pain, vomiting
GI bleeding leading to anemia
Development of colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or cervical cancer
sections.p: Complications stem from polyp burden and malignant transformation.

b: Endoscopic polypectomy for polyps < 2 cm to prevent obstruction
Surgical resection (segmental bowel resection) for large or symptomatic polyps
Annual breast MRI (or ultrasound in low‑resource settings) from age 25
Pancreatic imaging (MRI/MRCP) every 2–3 years after age 30
Counselling about 50 % lifetime cancer risk and need for family screening
sections.p: Treatment combines polyp control, cancer surveillance, and genetic counselling.

t.b: May reduce polyp size via COX‑2 inhibition; avoid in patients with cardiovascular disease
Supports bone health in patients with chronic malabsorption; no direct effect on polyps

b: Endoscopic review every 2–3 years, more often if polyps grow rapidly
Annual physical exam focusing on mucocutaneous spots and breast exam
Educate patients to report any new abdominal pain, change in stool colour, or breast lump promptly
sections.p: Lifelong surveillance is essential because cancer risk persists throughout adulthood.

b: Laugier‑Harlequin syndrome – isolated oral pigmentation without polyps
Familial adenomatous polyposis – numerous adenomatous polyps, no mucocutaneous spots
Cowden syndrome – hamartomas plus trichilemmomas, different cancer spectrum
sections.p: Conditions sharing pigmented mucosal lesions or polyps can mislead clinicians.

b: Normal colonoscopy does not exclude small‑bowel polyps; consider capsule endoscopy
Negative tumor markers do not rule out early malignancy; imaging remains crucial
sections.p: Certain investigations may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with vomiting (possible intussusception)
Profuse rectal bleeding or rapid drop in haemoglobin
New breast lump or palpable abdominal mass
